case_name: Board of Education of District No. 15 v. Human Rights Board of Inquiry (N.B.)
text:
New Brunswick School Dist. No. 15 v. New Brunswick (Human Rights Board of Inquiry)

1989-09-08

New Brunswick Court of Appeal Decision under the
HUMAN RIGHTS ACT, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11

The Minister of Labour and David Attis

Appellants

and

The Canadian Jewish Congress

Intervener

v.

The Board of School Trustees, District No. 15,
New Brunswick Teachers' Federation,
Human Rights Board of Inquiry, Human Rights Commission,
Department of Education, Malcolm Ross and Brian D. Bruce

Respondents

Date of Decisions:

September 8, 1989

Before:

Stratton, C.J.N.B. and Hoyt and Ryan JJ.A.

Reasons by:

Stratton C.J.N.B.

Dissenting reasons by:

Ryan J.A.

Court Action No.:

31/89/CA, 36/89/CA, 37/89/CA

Appeal from:

1989 CanLII 7931 (NB QB)
,
10 C.H.R.R. D/5800

Appearances by:

Gabriel Bourgeois, Counsel for the Appellant Minister of Labour

Joseph E. Weir, Counsel for the Appellant David Attis

Neil Finkelstein, Counsel for the Intervener Canadian Jewish Congress

James C. Letcher, Counsel for the Respondent Board of School Trustees, District No. 15

E. J. Mockler and Patrick Hurley, Counsel for the Respondent New Brunswick Teachers' Federation

Joanne E. McLeod and Thomas S. Kuttner, Counsel for the Respondent Human Rights Commission

Malcolm Ross on his own behalf

APPEALS AND JUDICIAL REVIEW — appeal of prohibition order — error of law in interpreting legislation — application to prevent hearing complaint by way of prohibition — review of court's power to order prohibition — ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNALS — COURTS — judicial review powers of court over administrative tribunals

PUBLIC SERVICES AND FACILITIES — discriminatory treatment in public school — definition of public services and facilities — EDUCATION — education facilities defined as public services or facilities — INTERPRETATION OF STATUTES — definition of "services . . . available to the public", "services or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted"

PARTIES — complainant not person directly discriminated against

Summary:
The New Brunswick Court of Appeal sets aside an order of the Court of Queen's Bench quashing the appointment of a Board of Inquiry to hear and decide the complaint of David Attis against the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15 and the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation.

David Attis filed a complaint under the New Brunswick Human Rights Act alleging that the School Board of District No. 15 condoned the racist views and activities of a teacher in its employ, Malcolm Ross, and by doing so deprived Jews and other minorities of an equal opportunity within the educational system that the School Board provides as a service to the public. David Attis is a Jew and he has two children enrolled in School District No. 15.

The Minister of Labour appointed a Board of Inquiry to hear Mr. Attis' complaint, but the School Board sought, and was granted, an order from the Court of Queen's Bench quashing the appointment of the Board of Inquiry on the grounds that education is not a public service within the meaning of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act and that Mr. Attis is not a proper complainant.

Before the Court of Appeal, there are three main issues: 1) is judicial review available to prohibit a Board of Inquiry from proceeding, 2) is education a public service within the meaning of section 5 of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act, and 3) is Mr. Attis a proper complainant.

The Court, in a decision authored by Chief Justice Stratton, finds that judicial review is available to prohibit a Board of Inquiry from proceeding, but only where the question regarding the Board's jurisdiction to hear a complaint turns on a question of law which can be determined apart from the facts of the case. In the present instance, the Court finds the questions regarding whether education is a service and whether Mr. Attis is a proper complainant are questions of law which can properly be determined by the court prior to any hearing by the Board of Inquiry. Therefore, the Court finds that the Court of Queen's Bench was correct in deciding that judicial review was available in this circumstance.

However, the Court of Appeal finds that the Court of Queen's Bench erred in finding that education is not a public service within the meaning of section 5 of the New Brunswick Human Rights Act. A purposive approach to the construction of the statute requires finding that the Act does apply to education. To hold otherwise would frustrate the legislative intent of the Act and ignore the broad purposive approach to anti-discrimination legislation adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada.

The Court of Appeal also finds that Mr. Attis is a proper complainant. A complaint may be filed by a "person claiming to be aggrieved" and Mr. Attis claims to be aggrieved by the School Board's actions.

In a minority concurring opinion, Ryan J.A. agrees with Chief Justice Stratton except with respect to his categorization of the status of the complainant as a question of law. Ryan states that the question of who qualifies as a person claiming to be aggrieved is almost wholly one of fact or at most a mixed question of fact and law. Ryan finds that this is a question of who is a proper complainant is one which a Board of Inquiry is well suited to answer. In his view, the Court of Queen's Bench ought not to have intervened to usurp the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry on this matter.

The Court of Appeal sets aside the order quashing the Board of Inquiry.

Stratton C.J.N.B.

[
1
]    There are essentially four issues raised by these three appeals: (1) Is judicial review available to prohibit a Board of Inquiry established under the
Human Rights Act, R.S.N.B.
1973, c. H-11, from proceeding with a hearing; (2) the interpretation to be given the
Human Rights Act
and, in particular, whether public education is governed by subsection 5(1) thereof; (3) the status of David Attis as a grievor under the
Act;
and (4) whether Mr. Attis' written complaint to the New Brunswick Human Rights Commission was sufficiently precise to constitute a valid complaint.

The Factual Background

[
2
]    On or about April 21, 1988, by a statement in writing on a form provided by and filed with the New Brunswick Human Rights Commission, the appellant David Attis complained against the respondent the Board of School Trustees of District No. 15. The complaint alleged discrimination under s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act
during the period March 29, 1977 to April 21, 1988.

[
3
]    Mr. Attis is a member of the Jewish community. Three of his children are enrolled as students in School District No. 15. He claims that by its statements and its inaction the School Board has condoned what he perceives to be the anti-Semitic and discriminatory views of Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed in School District No. 15. Mr. Attis alleges that Mr. Ross has publicized these views by making racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements to his students during the 1976–77 school year, through his writings in at least two books, and by widely published newspaper statements. Mr. Attis contends that the School Board has provided a racist and anti-Jewish role model for his students, has fostered a climate where students are at ease expressing anti-Jewish views, and has reduced the credibility of its official history curriculum, thus depriving Jewish and other minority students of equality of opportunity with respect to a public service.

[
4
]    In his written statement Mr. Attis said:

I am a Jew and three of my children are enrolled as students within District #15.

I have reason to believe that Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed by the School Board, made racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements to his students during the 1976–77 school year. I have reason to believe that the School Board knew of this, yet it merely transferred Malcolm Ross to another school.

Malcolm Ross has written at least two books (i.e. Webb of Deceit and Spectre of Power) and has made widely published statements (e.g.
Miramichi Leader,
October 22, 1986, page 5) that are anti-Jewish, racist, bigoted and discriminatory and that deny that six million Jews died during the Nazi Holocaust.

On April 22, 1987, the School Board failed to pass a motion condemning bigotry and racism. On March 15 or 16, 1988, Ray Maybee, a member of the School Board, publicly stated that Malcolm Ross' opinions were well documented and he had done his homework, thus appearing to support Mr. Ross' discriminatory views. Furthermore, when the School Board reprimanded Malcolm Ross on March 15, 1988, it referred to his views merely as controversial rather than discriminatory and the reprimand applied only to his future actions, not his past actions.

By its own statements and its inaction over Malcolm Ross' statements in class and in public, the School Board has condoned his views, has thus provided a racist and anti-Jewish role model for its students, has fostered a climate where students feel more at ease expressing anti-Jewish views, and has reduced the credibility of the content of its official history curriculum, thus depriving Jews and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system that the School Board provides as a service to the public.

I believe that the School Board has thus furthered the aims of the Mr. Rosses of our society. I would like to give a couple of examples:

i)    Several students at the Magnetic Hill School intend to present a petition to the Premier of New Brunswick in support of Malcolm Ross. When asked if they concurred with Ross' views, the students replied that they didn't know.

ii)    My eldest daughter, a grade 6 student at Beaverbrook School was invited by a friend to attend a gymnastic exhibition at Magnetic Hill School. She was reminded by a classmate that she shouldn't go there because that is "where the teacher who hates Jews" works. She attended nonetheless.

I have reasonable cause to believe that the Board of School Trustees of District #15 has violated Section 5 of the
Human Rights Act.

[
5
]    Upon receipt of Mr. Attis' written statement the Human Rights Commission, through a human rights officer, inquired into his allegations as required by s. 18 of the
Human Rights Act
and attempted to effect a settlement of the matter. However, no settlement was reached. On September 1, 1988, the Commission recommended to the provincial Minister of Labour that a Board of Inquiry be appointed to investigate the matter as provided by s. 20 of the
Act.
On that same day, the Minister appointed Professor Brian D. Bruce of the Faculty of Law at the University of New Brunswick as the Board of Inquiry.

[
6
]    The Board of Inquiry was scheduled to hold its first hearing on November 21, 1988. On November 17, 1988, Mr. Justice Miller of the Court of Queen's Bench ordered a stay of proceedings by the Board of Inquiry pending the final disposition of two applications for judicial review filed by the school board and the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation seeking to prohibit the Board from proceeding with its inquiry.

The Decision Appealed From

[
7
]    In a decision dated January 19, 1989, Mr. Justice Miller granted the applications for judicial review and quashed the order of the Minister of Labour which had established the Board of Inquiry. In the course of his reasons for decision, Miller J. made three pivotal rulings. First, he held that in appropriate circumstances a court has the power to order that an established administrative tribunal be prohibited from acting. He observed however, that this power is to be exercised with extreme caution; but, he said if an applicant can properly raise an issue of law then the applicant can seek a prohibition order by way of judicial review prior to the tribunal undertaking its inquiry. Second, he held that the provision of school facilities and an education program are not included within the meaning of "accommodation, services and facilities" as found in s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act.
Third, the judge of first instance held that the allegations in the written statement filed by Mr. Attis were not specific enough to qualify as a complaint within the meaning of the
Act.
He pointed out that the Board of Inquiry must not only know what it is being asked to consider, but the School Board against whom the complaint is made must know what allegations it faces. He added too that a representative claim is not envisaged by the
Act.
The legislation, he said, can only be set in motion by a proper complaint from an aggrieved party alleging discrimination within the provisions of the statute.

[
8
]    From the decision of Miller J. three separate appeals were filed in this Court. But all three appeals involve the same issues and were consolidated and heard on the same date. In my opinion, only one decision is necessary to dispose of all three appeals.

The Arguments

[
9
]    The Minister of Labour, Mr. David Attis, the Human Rights Commission and the Canadian Jewish Congress submit that Miller J. erred by usurping the Board of Inquiry's statutorily assigned rights and duties to hear and adjudicate upon the matter. These parties further contend that the judge misinterpreted s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act
as not including educational services rendered by the New Brunswick public school system and incorrectly held that the complaint was too imprecise and that Mr. Attis was not a person aggrieved under the
Act.
They further contend that the trial judge's findings of fact were too extensive based only on affidavit evidence on an application for judicial review, and the quashing of the Minister's order was incorrect since the Minister had exercised an administrative function that could not be the subject of a judicial review order of that nature. Finally, David Attis argues that the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation lost any right it may have had to request a judicial review order by seeking participation in the formal hearing of the Board of Inquiry.

[
10
]    On the other hand, the Board of School Trustees, the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation and Malcolm Ross submit that if the complaint is not a proper complaint then that decision is a question of law that does not depend upon the finding of certain facts. Further, they submit, Miller J. was correct in construing s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act
as not including educational services rendered by the public school system; in holding that the complaint of David Attis does not describe a discriminatory situation; and in deciding that Mr. Attis was not the object of personal discrimination and was purporting to speak on behalf of a group. Moreover, the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation submits that it has standing to question the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry on judicial review as a party to the inquiry.

Discussion

I.    Introduction

[
11
]    I think it is of singular importance at the outset of these reasons to state what the Court is called upon to decide in these three appeals and, of equal importance, what it is not called upon to decide. It has been asked to decide the availability of judicial review, the interpretation of s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act,
the status of David Attis as a complainant and the sufficiency of the complaint. It has not been called upon to decide, or even to enter, the clamorous and continuing public debate concerning the published writings and public statements of Malcolm Ross.

II.    Availability of Judicial Review

[
12
]    An application for judicial review to prohibit an administrative tribunal from proceeding may be sought as soon as an absence of jurisdiction has either arisen or may clearly be foreseen. The main advantage of such an application is that it may be brought to test the validity of proceedings before they are undertaken with a possible saving of time and expense. However, an application for judicial review to prevent an apprehended error of law may be premature where the tribunal has not yet had a chance to find facts on which its jurisdiction depends; see Robert Reid
Administrative Law and Practice,
2d ed., (Toronto: Carswell, 1978) at 340–341. The guiding principle would seem to be that where there is a clear question of law not depending upon particular facts, there is no reason why an applicant should not go directly to the court for a judicial review order prohibiting a tribunal from proceeding rather than waiting to see if the decision goes against him, in which case he would then have to move to quash the decision: see
R.
v.
Tottenham and District Rent Tribunal,

[1957] 1 Q.B. 103
, per Lord Goddard C.J., at 108.

[
13
]    The decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Bell
v.
Ontario Human Rights Commission,

1971 CanLII 195 (SCC)
,
[1971] S.C.R. 756
was relied upon by the judge of first instance as authority for the granting of an order of prohibition in the circumstances of the present case.
In
Bell
,
the majority of the Court held that prohibition was available to prevent proceedings investigating a complaint under the
Ontario Human Rights Code
involving a question of law. Mr. Justice Martland, speaking for the majority, described the interrelationship between facts and law for such an application at pp. 774–775:

The present case raises a question of law as to the meaning of the phrase "self-contained dwelling unit." The facts involved in relation to whether or not the appellant's premises available for rent were within that phrase relate only to the structure of a building and
do not involve choosing between the conflicting testimony of witnesses. In a case involving a conflict of evidence a Court to which an application for prohibition was made might well decline to interfere. . . .

The powers given to a board of inquiry are to enable it to determine whether or not there has been discrimination in respect of matters within the scope of the Act. It has no power to deal with alleged discrimination in matters not within the purview of the Act or to make recommendations with respect thereto. . . .

In my opinion
the appellant was not compelled to await the decision of the board on that issue before seeking to have it determined in a court of law by an application for prohibition and the Court had jurisdiction to deal with the matter.
[Emphasis added.]

[
14
]    In a subsequent decision,
Re CIP Paper Products Ltd.
v.
Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

(1978),
1978 CanLII 1847 (SK CA)
,
87 D.L.R. (3d) 609
, Chief Justice Culliton, speaking for the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, attempted to limit the application of the
Bell
decision.
He wrote at p. 612:

Care must be taken not to give to
the decision in
Bell
v.
Ontario Human Rights Commission
too wide an application.
That case simply decided that, where there is a clear point of law not depending upon particular facts upon the determination of which the jurisdiction of the tribunal depends, that determination may be made in an application for prohibition.
That judgment did not decide that prohibition lies on the contention that the complaint is one which cannot be sustained within the provisions of the Act in respect to which the complaint is made. The decision as to whether the complaint is one which is contemplated by the pertinent legislation, and, if so, whether discrimination is, or is not, established, are matters for the Human Rights Commission. Such statutory rights and duties of the Commission cannot be usurped by the Court under the guise of prohibition proceedings in which is sought, in effect, a determination of the complaint on its merits. [Emphasis added.]

[
15
]    It is perhaps trite to note that there are numerous authoritative decisions which have directed courts to exercise restraint and curial deference when dealing with the specialized jurisdiction confided to statutory tribunals. It has been said that a court ought not to preempt a statutory tribunal nor usurp its rights and duties under the guise of prohibition proceedings. Nor should a court be astute to hold that Parliament did not intend the tribunal to have jurisdiction to decide for itself the meaning of ordinary words used in the statute to define the question which it has to decide. On the other hand, it has also been said that it is a jurisdictional error for a human rights commission to set up an inquiry when the subject matter of the inquiry cannot involve a contravention of the
Act
: see
Re Alberta Human Rights Commission
v.
The Queen

(1986),
1986 ABCA 32 (CanLII)
,
27 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Alta. C.A.)
at 736
.

[
16
]    The non-interventionist approach to judicial review of administrative bodies enunciated by the courts was recently considered by Madam Justice L'Heureux-Dubé, dissenting, in
Telecommunication Workers Union
v.
British Columbia Telephone Company,

1988 CanLII 14 (SCC)
,
[1988], 2 S.C.R. 564
. She said at p. 593:

The deferential approach is not a licence to refuse review. It is merely a caution to courts to recognize the proper role and function of administrative bodies. When such bodies fail to act within jurisdiction, the Court does not have the
discretion
to intervene, it has a
duty
to intervene at the behest of one or another of the parties. [Emphasis in original.]

[
17
]    Turning now to the present case, it is my opinion that the three major grounds of appeal, namely, the interpretation of s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act,
the status of Mr. Attis as a complainant under the
Act
and the sufficiency of the complaint as measured against the statutory requirements of the
Act
are questions of law that do not concern the determination of facts upon which the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry depends. Although it could perhaps be argued that the latter two grounds of appeal involve contested facts, it is my opinion that the Court can restrict itself to the questions of law dependent upon the uncontested facts adduced by affidavit evidence.

[
18
]    I am satisfied that the judge in the present case did not, either directly or indirectly, attempt to decide the merits of the Attis complaint. Rather, he concluded there were clear questions of law to be decided, particularly the meaning of the phrase "accommodation, services and facilities" contained in s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act.
While it is clear that "the courts should not be alert to brand as jurisdictional, and therefore subject to broader curial review, that which may be doubtfully so" (per Dickson J. in
Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 963
v.
New Brunswick Liquor Corporation,

1979 CanLII 23 (SCC)
,
[1979] 2 S.C.R. 227
at 233)
, I am not persuaded that the Judge, who exercised his discretion in favour of granting an order of prohibition in this instance, did so for any improper reason.

[
19
]    As previously noted, Mr. David Attis has also challenged the status of the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation to apply for judicial review to prohibit the Board of Inquiry from proceeding. Mr. Attis argues that by seeking to participate in the inquiry as a party, the Federation acquiesced in the Board's jurisdiction and could not subsequently challenge that jurisdiction by means of judicial review. With respect, I can find no merit in this argument. Acquiescence means participation in proceedings without taking objection to the jurisdiction of the tribunal once the facts for raising the objection are fully known: see S. A. Smith
Judicial Review of Administrative Action,
4th ed. (London: Stevens, 1980) at 423.

[
20
]    In the present case the Teachers' Federation sought status as a party at the inquiry prior to the Board convening its first hearing. At the earliest opportunity it then made an application for judicial review based on the jurisdictional issue. I see no parallel between the present appeals and
Re Colonial Coach Lines Ltd.
v.
Ontario Highway Transport Board

(1967),
1967 CanLII 185 (ON CA)
,
63 D.L.R. (2d) 198, (Ont. C.A.)
. In that case, the hearings were well in progress when the applicant pressed the Board to make a decision on jurisdiction. Before the Board could decide the matter, the applicant served notice of prohibition proceedings. In my view, there is no similar high-handed conduct by the Teachers' Federation in its application that could be relevant in determining whether an order of prohibition should lie.

[
21
]    Having concluded that this is a case which lent itself to judicial review, I turn now to a consideration of the remaining issues, namely, the scope of s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act,
the status of Mr. Attis as a complainant and the sufficiency of the complaint.

III.    Interpretation of Section 5 of the Human Rights Act

[
22
]    A pivotal question in the present case is whether subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act
includes education in the New Brunswick public school system.
Subsection 5(1)
of the
Human Rights Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. H-11 stated:

5.(1)      No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(a)      deny to any person or class of persons the accommodation, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted, or

(b)      discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to the accommodations, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, marital status or sex.

[
23
]    The current subsection 5(1) as amended by
An Act to Amend the Human Rights Act,
S.N.B. 1985, c. C-30 s. 7 states:

5.(1)      No person, directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of another, shall

(a)      deny to any person or class of persons any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public, or

(b)      discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public,

because of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, physical disability, mental disability, marital status or sex.

[
24
]    It will be observed that the major change which has occurred in the subsection is that the phrase "the accommodation, services, or facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted" has been amended to read "any accommodation, services or facilities available to the public." It could be argued that this alteration broadens the application of the provision.

[
25
]    In
Gay Alliance Toward Equality
v.
Vancouver Sun,

1979 CanLII 225 (SCC)
,
[1979] 2 S.C.R. 435
, the Supreme Court of Canada was called upon to interpret s. 3 of the
Human Rights Code
of British Columbia, S.B.C.
1984, c. 22
, which prohibited discrimination with respect to "any accommodation, service or facility customarily available to the public." Martland J., speaking for the majority of the Court, gave some examples of the three terms used in the section. He said at p. 455:

"Accommodation" refers to such matters as accommodation in hotels, inns and motels. "Service" refers to such matters as restaurants, bars, taverns, service stations, public transportation and public utilities. "Facility" refers to such matters as public parks and recreational facilities. These are all items "customarily available to the public."

[
26
]    The majority of the Court in the
Gay Alliance
case concluded that s. 3 of the British Columbia
Human Rights Code
did not purport to dictate the nature and scope of a service which must be offered to the public. Nor do I read the judgment as holding that the examples which were given for "accommodation," "service" and "facility" constitute an exhaustive list.

[
27
]    In the current decade, the Supreme Court of Canada has consistently adopted an expansive interpretive approach to human rights codes and acts. In
Insurance Corp. of British Columbia
v.
Heerspink,

1982 CanLII 27 (SCC)
,
[1982] 2 S.C.R. 145
at 158,
[3 C.H.R.R. D/1163 at D/1166], Lamer J. characterized a human rights code as "a fundamental law." In
Ontario Human Rights Commission and O'Malley
v.
Simpsons-Sears Ltd.,

1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 536
, [7 C.H.R.R. D/3102], McIntyre J. set forth the governing principles in the interpretation of human rights statutes as follows, at 546–547 [S.C.R., D/3105 C.H.R.R.]:

It is not . . . a sound approach to say that according to established rules of construction no broader meaning can be given to the
Code
than the narrowest interpretation of the words employed. The accepted rules of construction are flexible enough to enable the Court to recognize in the construction of a human rights code the special nature and purpose of the enactment . . . and give it an interpretation which will advance its broad purposes. Legislation of this type is of a special nature, not quite constitutional, but certainly more than the ordinary — and it is for the courts to seek out its purpose and give it effect. The
Code
aims at the removal of discrimination.

[
28
]    The purposive approach in construing human rights statutes has been followed by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Bhinder
v.
Canadian National Railway Co.,

1985 CanLII 19 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 561
, [7 C.H.R.R. D/3093];
Action travail des femmes
v.
Canadian National Railway Co.
(
sub nom. Canadian National Railway Co.
v.
Canada (Canadian Human Rights Commission)
),
1987 CanLII 109 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R 1114
,
76 N.R. 161
, 8 C.H.R.R. D/4210; and
Robichaud
v.
Canada (Treasury Board),

1987 CanLII 73 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2 S.C.R. 84
, 8 C.H.R.R. D/4326, 40 D.L.R. (4th) 577, 75 N.R. 303.
In
Robichaud
,
La Forest J. declared at p. 89 [S.C.R., D/4329 C.H.R.R.]:

[T]he Act must be so interpreted as to advance the broad policy considerations underlying it. That task should not be approached in a niggardly fashion but in a manner befitting the special nature of the legislation.

[
29
]    In
Re Winnipeg School Division No. 1
v.
MacArthur

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2975 (MB QB)
,
133 D.L.R. (3d) 305
, [
1982 CanLII 4893 (MB QB)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/917
] (Man. Q.B.), a decision relied upon by the judge of first instance, Kroft J. held that a public school was not an "accommodation, service or facility" within the meaning of the
Manitoba
Human Rights Act.
In contrast Shannon J. of the Alberta Supreme Court held in
Re Schmidt
v.
Calgary Board of Education

(1975),
1975 CanLII 254 (AB SCTD)
,
57 D.L.R. (3d) 746
; rev'd on other grounds
(1976),
1976 ALTASCAD 157 (CanLII)
,
72 D.L.R. (3d) 330, (Alta. C.A.)
that a broad and liberal interpretation permitted public schools to fall within a similar provision.

[
30
]    In
Rawala
v.
DeVry Institute of Technology

(1982),
1982 CanLII 4880 (ON HRT)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/1057
, an Ontario board of inquiry ruled that a private educational institute was a service or facility provided in a place to which the public was customarily admitted. This case was, however, distinguished in
Sonnenberg
v.
Centre universitaire St-Louis-Maillet

(1988),
1987 CanLII 8588 (NB BHR)
,
9 C.H.R.R. D/5100
. In the latter decision, a New Brunswick Board of Inquiry explained that
in the
Rawala
case the premises were found to be public since the Institute offered its facilities to the public and advertised while the
Centre
did not advertise or promote the use of its facilities.

[
31
]    Thus, it seems clear that the question whether public or private education is governed by human rights legislation is not yet settled. It is my opinion, however, that the
New Brunswick Human Rights Act
is cast in wide terms and both its subject matter and its stated purpose suggest that it is not to be interpreted narrowly or restrictively: see
Re

Attorney General of Canada
v.
Cumming

(1980),
1979 CanLII 4104 (FC)
,
103 D.L.R. (3d) 151
, [
1979 CanLII 4118 (FCA)
,
1 C.H.R.R. D/91
], per Thurlow C.J., at 158, [D.L.R., D/94 C.H.R.R.]. When one gives to subsection 5(1) of the
Act
a "fair, large and liberal interpretation" as required by
s. 17
of the
Interpretation Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, it would, I think, undoubtedly bring public education within its purview. To hold otherwise would seem to me to frustrate the legislative intent of the
Human Rights Act
and its preamble and amount to a rejection of the broad purposive approach to the interpretation of anti-discrimination legislation adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada. As Mr. Justice Walter S. Tarnopolsky and William F. Pentney reasoned in their text
Discrimination and the Law,
(Toronto: R. DeBoo, 1985) at 11–47:

The two preceding decisions, [
Winnipeg School Division No. 1
v.
McArthur; Rawala and Souza
v.
DeVry Institute of Technology
], illustrate the remarkable state of Canadian law with respect to services and facilities customarily available to the public. In Manitoba a public school is found not to be such a service or facility, while in Ontario a private school is brought within the scope of the legislation. It is respectfully submitted that the
McArthur
decision is incorrect. In support of this view one need only point out that if this decision is correct, a public school in Manitoba would not contravene the
Human Rights Act
by refusing entrance to Indian (or Jewish or male) children. Surely such an interpretation was not intended by the drafters of the Act nor is it necessary in order to ensure the effective application of the law.

[
32
]    As an alternative basis for my conclusion that public education is governed by subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act,
I would adopt the reasoning of the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal in
Saskatchewan (Human Rights Comm.
v.
Saskatchewan (Dept. of Social Services

(1988),
1988 CanLII 212 (SK CA)
,
52 D.L.R. (4th) 253
, [9 C.H.R.R. D/5181].In that case, the Court held that social assistance provided under the
Saskatchewan Assistance Act
was a service which was offered to the public and thus was affected by the
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code
even though there were criteria for eligibility for assistance. Vancise J.A. explained at 268 [D.L.R., D/5185 C.H.R.R.] that the fact that a service is offered to the public does not mean that it must be offered to all members of the public. The government can impose eligibility requirements to ensure that the program or services reaches the intended client group. The only restriction is that the government cannot discriminate among the members of the client group on the basis of the prohibited grounds contained in the human rights legislation. Applying the principles enunciated in this case to the present appeals, I would hold that public education provided under the
Schools Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. S-5, is a service available to the public. It is a service provided to a client group, the members of which meet the eligibility requirements specified in the
Schools Act.
Thus, on this alternative basis, I would also conclude that public education falls within the purview of subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act.

IV.    Status of Complainant

[
33
]    In his reasons for decision, the judge of first instance appears to indicate that David Attis was not an aggrieved party alleging discrimination within the
Human Rights Act.
He held that although Mr. Attis is a member of the Jewish community in School District No. 15, the affidavit evidence was that neither he nor his children had ever had direct contact with Mr. Ross as a teacher. I would pause here to note that a trial judge must be careful on an application for judicial review not to rely too heavily upon the limited facts before him in making his decision, otherwise he risks deciding the merits of the case.

[
34
]    It is argued that David Attis should be given status as a complainant because he is a parent of children enrolled in School District No. 15. The authority upon which this argument is based is
Société des Acadiens
v.
Minority Language School Board

(1984),
1984 CanLII 2954 (NB CA)
,
54 N.B.R. (2d) 198, (N.B.C.A.)
; aff'd
(1986),
1986 CanLII 66 (SCC)
,
69 N.B.R. (2d) 271, (S.C.C.)
. In that matter, the Association of Parents for Fairness in Education, formed by some forty parents, moved for leave to appeal as an intended intervener and requested an extension of time within which to file a notice of appeal. This Court granted an order that the Association be given leave to appeal as a defendant in the case. The Court was persuaded to issue the order by the parental status of the members of the Association, but the legal foundations for the order were the
Rules of Court,
the
Judicature Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. J-2, and in particular
s. 8(2)
thereof, and the inherent jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal. Analytically, I find the application of this precedent to these appeals to be inappropriate because of the distinction between status in court proceedings, and status as a complainant under the
Human Rights Act.

[
35
]    In order to discover if Mr. Attis is a proper complainant reference must be made to s. 17 of the
Human Rights Act
:

17.          Any person claiming to be aggrieved because of an alleged violation of this Act may make a complaint in writing to the Commission in a form prescribed by the Commission.

[
36
]    I agree with the submission that the phrase "any person claiming to be aggrieved" in s. 17 should be given a wide interpretation. This is particularly so at a preliminary stage before the Board of Inquiry has held a hearing into the facts. As
stated by Hugessen J.A., in
Re Singh

(1988),
1988 CanLII 5665 (FCA)
,
86 N.R. 69
, [
1988 CanLII 8967 (FCA)
,
10 C.H.R.R. D/5501
] (F.C.A.) at 77 [N.R., D/5510 C.H.R.R.]:

The question as to who is the "victim" of an alleged discriminatory practice is almost wholly one of fact. Human rights legislation does not look so much to the intent of discriminatory practices as to their effect. . . . That effect is by no means limited to the alleged "target" of the discrimination and it is entirely conceivable that a discriminatory practice may have consequences which are sufficiently direct and immediate to justify qualifying as a "victim" thereof persons who were never within the contemplation or intent of its author.

[
37
]    Mr. Attis made a written complaint to the Commission on a form prescribed by the Commission. The section does not refer to the person filing the complaint as an aggrieved party, as the trial Judge stated, but as a "person claiming to be aggrieved." The Legislature has decided that it is for the Commission and a board of inquiry to discover if there is any merit in a claim of discrimination. Thus, I would conclude that Mr. Attis has met the statutory standard in
s. 17
to be accorded the legal status of complainant.

[
38
]    The question has also been raised whether David Attis was intending to make a representative complaint because he alleges the School Board has deprived "Jews and other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system that the School Board provides as a service to the public." In
Lévesque and Tardif
v.
The Daily Gleaner,
(September 10, 1974) [unreported], a New Brunswick Board of Inquiry held that the two complainants could not bring a complaint on behalf of all French New Brunswickers because of the restricted definition of "person" contained in the
Act.
This decision was criticized by an Ontario Board of Inquiry in
Tabar and Lee
v.
Scott and West End Construction Ltd.

(1982),
1982 CanLII 4887 (ON HRT)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/1073
. Peter A. Cumming remarked at D/1076:

If there is no means by which a class of persons may enforce their rights, such rights would be rendered nugatory. The board in
Lévesque,
in effect, repealed the provisions in the New Brunswick Act that prohibited discrimination against a class of persons.

[
39
]    But this issue does not have to be decided in the present appeals since the Minister of Labour recognizes that there are no rules applicable to the
Human Rights Act
that would permit group actions, and David Attis claims that the major thrust and intent of his complaint is not representative, but that the School Board has discriminated against him and his children.

V.    Sufficiency of the Complaint

[
40
]    The procedures of the Commission respecting transgressions against the
Human Rights Act
are triggered by a complaint under s. 17. Miller J., held that the Attis complaint lacked the requisite specificity. In reaching that conclusion, he relied upon the decision of this Court in
Mackin
v.
Judicial Council (N.B.)

(1988),
1987 CanLII 138 (NB CA)
,
82 N.B.R. (2d) 203
, as defining the necessary standard for a complaint. In that case, the Attorney-General of New Brunswick wrote a letter of "complaint" to the Chairman of the Judicial Council concerning the conduct of a Provincial Court judge. The Judicial Council directed that an inquiry be held "into the complaint and the report." The majority of the Court of Appeal granted an application for judicial review for a prohibition order because in the opinion of the majority the Attorney General's letter fell short of being a complaint.

[
41
]    It is my opinion, however, that the requirements for a complaint under the
Provincial Court Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-21, to commence an inquiry concerning the conduct of a Provincial Court judge are not the same as the requirements for a complaint under the
Human Rights Act
because of the special nature and purpose of the latter enactment. The word "complaint" as used in s. 17 of the
Human Rights Act
must be given an interpretation which will advance the broad purposes of the
Act,
i.e. the advancement of human rights and the elimination of discrimination.

[
42
]    In
Canada (Canadian Human Rights Comm.)
v.
Bell Canada

(1981),
1981 CanLII 4292 (CHRT)
,
2 C.H.R.R. D/265
, the tribunal held that any valid complaint under the
Canadian Human Rights Act
must contain several elements. These included identification of the complainant, identification of the victim, the time during which the alleged violation took place, the location of the alleged violation, the nature of the discriminatory practice, the relevant section of the
Act,
and an affirmation by the complainant and/or the Commission that they have reasonable grounds to believe that the conduct constituted a discriminatory practice which violated the
Act.

[
43
]    The Attis complaint appears to me to meet the statutory requirements of
s. 17
that it be in writing and on a form prescribed by the Commission, and that it contains most of the essential elements referred to above. On an application for judicial review this, in my opinion, is sufficient to classify David Attis' written submission to the Commission as a complaint under the
Act.
If further information is required during the proceedings before the Board of Inquiry then a demand for particulars can be made. Pursuant to s. 20(3) of the
Human Rights Act,
a board of inquiry has all the powers of a conciliation board which may determine its own procedure under
subsection 66(2)
of the
Industrial Relations Act,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-4.

[
44
]    It is perhaps unnecessary to point out that it is the function of the Board of Inquiry and not of a reviewing court to investigate the merits of a complaint. I would, however, repeat the remarks of Thurlow C.J. in the
Cummings
decision that in cases like the present one, it is usually preferable for the Court to leave the tribunal free to carry out its mandate except when it is clear and beyond doubt that the tribunal is without jurisdiction to deal with the matter before it. In my opinion, the present case is not within the exception.

VI.    Appropriateness of the Judicial Review Order

[
45
]    In his decision, Miller J. purported to quash the order of the Minister of Labour which established the Board of Inquiry. In issuing the order, the Minister was acting in an administrative capacity. Therefore, the quashing of his order was not available as a remedy in these proceedings: see
Hawley
v.
Richmond County Municipal School Board

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2943 (NS CA)
,
52 N.S.R. (2d) 127 (N.S.C.A.)
and
Mehta
v.
MacKinnon

(1985),
1985 CanLII 3117 (NS SC)
,
67 N.S.R. (2d) 429
, [6 C.H.R.R. D/2861] (N.S.C.A.). The order should have been expressed as prohibiting the Board of Inquiry from proceeding.

VII.    Conclusion

[
46
]    In summary, it is my opinion that this is a case in which the judge of first instance could properly exercise his jurisdiction in favour of granting judicial review; that public education in New Brunswick is within the purview of subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act;
that David Attis does have status as a complainant, and that the written submission which he filed with the Commission is a complaint under the
Act.

[
47
]    For all of the foregoing reasons, I would allow the three appeals and set aside the order purporting to quash the order of the Minister of Labour, thereby permitting the Board of Inquiry to proceed. In the circumstances, I would make no order as to cost.

Ryan J.A.

[
48
]    I have read the reasons for judgment of Chief Justice Stratton and concur with him except with respect to his categorization of the status of the complainant and the sufficiency of the complaint as questions of law.

[
49
]    Any person claiming to be aggrieved may file a written complaint on a form provided by the Human Rights Commission. It seems to me that the question of who qualifies as a "person claiming to be aggrieved" is almost wholly one of fact, that is, a combination of fact and law. In a purist form of inquiry both questions under review may qualify as questions of law when measured only against the statutory requirement of the
Human Rights Act
but in this case I do not think that they ought to be considered in such a narrow environment. As well, I believe that status and sufficiency questions are matters which the Commission, or in this case the board of inquiry, is well suited to answer. The Court of Queen's Bench ought not to have intervened on these two grounds thus aborting the legislative mandate of the Human Rights Commission, or its board, as to who is a complainant and whether the contents of the form filed constitute a complaint.

[
50
]    The main purpose of a human rights commission is to investigate complaints of discrimination within the scope of the
Human Rights Act.
Since this is its purpose the courts should not goaltend access to the tribunal. On the contrary, the courts should defer to the jurisdiction of the tribunal so that effect can be given to its purpose. I hold this same view whether the legislative intent of the Act in question is remedial, with punitive powers, or punitive alone.

[
51
]    However, I agree with the Chief Justice of New Brunswick that the judge of first instance properly exercised his jurisdiction on judicial review on a question of law with respect to the issue of public education, albeit the judge of first instance came to an erroneous result in finding that the public education system of New Brunswick is not included within the term "services" under s. 5 of the
Human Rights Act.
This erroneous decision in law, which does not concern the determination of facts, was the proper subject of appeal for reversal by this Court. For the reasons given by the Chief Justice with respect to the interpretation of s. 5, the appeal should be allowed.
